title: The OI class
summary: static methods on an abstract class that owns the controller.

say.never:
`OI` stands for **Operator Interface**, which is just a fancy name for "the controls". This class is the only place that knows about the gamepad. The rest of the robot asks it questions like "how far forward is the driver pushing?" and never cares which stick that comes from. Nobody ever makes a new OI, and its methods are `static`, so you call them on the class itself.

The picture: robot code asks OI "how hard is the driver pushing forward?", and OI reads the gamepad. Only OI knows which stick that is.
say.bit: OI (Operator Interface) is the one class that knows about the gamepad. The rest of the robot asks it questions through static methods.

It looks like this: `public abstract class OI {` holds a private `XboxController`, and a method like `public static double getForward()` returns a stick value. `abstract` means nobody ever writes `new OI()`. `static` means you call the method on the class itself, as `OI.getForward()`.
say.bit: `OI` (Operator Interface) owns the controller and answers questions about it. `abstract` means nobody writes `new OI()`, and `static` means you call `OI.getForward()` on the class.
